The lighthouse had not been lit in forty years, and the town had stopped looking at it.

Ivy Calder came back in November, when the sea was the colour of old iron. She had her mother's keys in her coat pocket, three of them on a loop of wire, and she had not decided yet whether she would use them. The road out to the point was gone in places. Where it had fallen away she walked on the shingle, and the stones moved under her like something breathing.

Her mother had been the last keeper. People in the town still said it that way, the last keeper, as though there had been a ceremony. There had not. There had been a letter from the department, and a van that came for the equipment, and a winter when nobody spoke to them in the shop.

The door at the base of the tower was swollen shut. Ivy put her shoulder to it twice before it gave, and the smell that came out was salt and cold stone and something older underneath. She climbed. Ninety-seven steps, and she counted them the way she had when she was nine, and the count came out right, which surprised her more than anything else had that day.

The lamp room was full of grey light. The great lens sat under a dust sheet, and when she pulled the sheet away the prisms threw weak rainbows onto the wall, and for a moment the whole room looked like it was underwater.

She found her mother's log book on the sill, swollen with damp, the last entry in November forty years ago. It said: wind southwest, visibility poor, lamp lit at four. Nothing after that. Ivy sat down on the cold floor with the book in her lap and stayed there until the light went.
